title: Scottish Labour demands SNP plan to avoid £5bn budget black hole
excerpt: Scottish Labour has demanded an SNP budget plan to tackle a projected £5bn spending gap by 2030, protect public services and provide £350 energy bill support.
content:
Scottish Labour has called on the SNP Government to set out a plan to avoid a £5 billion spending gap as it unveiled its priorities for next month's Budget.

The party has demanded greater transparency over the state of Scotland's public finances, alongside measures to protect public services and support struggling households.

Scottish Labour's finance spokesman Joe Fagan said ministers must explain how they intend to close the projected spending gap by 2030 without cutting vital services.

The demands come ahead of the Scottish Government's Budget on December 3, when ministers will set out their tax and spending plans.

Labour wants the Budget to protect funding for councils, colleges, Police Scotland and the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, while setting out a strategy to grow the economy and strengthen the public finances.

The party is also calling for business rates support announced by the UK Labour Government to be passed on to Scottish high streets.

It wants ministers to guarantee £350 in energy bill support for the poorest households this winter, using funding linked to UK Government energy payments.

Other demands include increased investment in drug and alcohol services, funded through a proposed windfall tax on excess profits made from alcohol sales by major supermarkets.

Labour is also calling for a greater emphasis on preventative spending, aimed at tackling problems before they place further pressure on public services.

Mr Fagan said: "The UK Labour government has delivered £18 billion of additional funding for the Scottish budget since coming to power.

"We shouldn't be in a position where public services like councils, colleges, police and fire are facing cuts.

"Our high streets need more support and the budget should deliver £350 of support for the poorest households this winter by passing on all the funding related to UK Labour's energy payment.

"We also need to get extra resource into the NHS to tackle the national scandal of drug and alcohol deaths, we can do that by asking the biggest supermarkets to pay their fair share of excess profits generated by alcohol sales."

Mr Fagan argued that the Scottish Government must take steps to address longer-term pressures on public spending rather than relying on short-term measures.

He added: "This budget must also set out a plan for growth that fixes the foundations of Scotland's finances for the long term.

"Holyrood faces a £5 billion spending gap in 2030. We need transparency on the state of the finances and how that gap is closed without cuts to services that people rely on."

The Scottish Government has said they are engaging with opposition parties ahead of the Scottish Budget.

A Scottish Government spokesperson said: "The DFM has been engaging with opposition parties and we welcome these constructive suggestions. The draft Budget will be published on 3 December."
